id="Sec2"><title>Synonyms</title><p>Nematode; Worm; Genetic control of behavior</p></sec><sec id="Sec3"><title>Definition</title><p>In 1974, Sidney Brenner first introduced the nematode <italic toggle="yes">Caenorhabditis elegan</italic>s as a model for studies of the genetic control of nervous systems and behavior [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1">1</xref>]. Since then, a great deal of research has been focused on this 1 mm long roundworm. With its small nervous system, and fully sequenced genome, <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> is an excellent system in which to investigate the cellular mechanisms of behaviors such as foraging, feeding, defecation, movement, egg-laying, male mating behavior, sensory responses to touch, smell, taste and temperature, as well as simple forms of learning. It has a small and tractable nervous system, which consists of 302 neurons and approximately 5,000 chemical synapses [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2">2</xref>]. Every neuron has been identified, its cell lineage traced and it connectivity patterns mapped [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2">2</xref>]. Many of the <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> genes involved in coding its neural machinery are 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8 to those in other organisms [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3">3</xref>], including neurotransmitters, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_7 and many metabolic pathways. Many different strategies are used to study neuroethology in <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>, including detailed behavioral analyses, laser ablation of identified neurons and mutants with alterations in genes expressed in specific neurons to determine the neural circuits underlying the behavior, genetic screens to determine genes involved in the behavior, modern genetic techniques to determine gene expression patterns and patterns of gene interaction. In this review, we will highlight several sensory behaviors, behavior plasticity and a foraging behavior as examples of how <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> can be used for studies of neural and genetic analyses of behavior.</p></sec><sec id="Sec4"><title>Characteristics</title><sec id="Sec5"><title>Higher Level Processes: Modes of Sensory Input</title><p>Studies of the behavior and anatomy of <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> have determined that <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> has three major types of sensory receptors: chemoreceptors, thermoreceptors and mechanosensory receptors [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3">3</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> behavior and its ability to adapt to environmental cues are mediated by these three modes of sensory input, and allows for interesting investigations into the neural circuitry and genetic pathways that underlie these systems.</p></sec><sec id="Sec6"><title>Lower Level Process: Chemotaxis</title><p>Studies investigating chemotactic behavior have used behavioral analysis, genetic manipulation and laser ablation (killing) of specific neurons to lead to the identification of the 22 specific chemosensory neurons necessary for <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> to detect and respond to different chemical cues [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4">4</xref>]. The 11 pairs of chemosensory neurons located in the anterior amphid sensillum (nose; see Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>) have been divided into two separate classes responsible for either the sensation of taste or smell.<fig id="Fig1" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>C. elegans Neuroethology. Figure 1</label><caption><p>Drawing of <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> showing some of the elements of the neural circuitry involved in chemotactic, thermotactic, and mechanosensory behaviors; sensory neurons represented by triangles; interneurons represented by circles; motor neurons represented by squares. The neurons shown are representative of the neurons used for these behaviors, not all neurons in the circuits described in the text are drawn.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e2598" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig1_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig1_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 45423?><?image-md5 338b77b560ee48e2707919ee3ed642d3?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 200?><?image-original-width 480?><?image-scaled-height 200?><?image-scaled-width 480?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/338b77b560ee/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig1_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig1_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 11646?><?thumb-md5 a5df3430d8dd9cf9b80355d106b926f3?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 192?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/a5df3430d8dd/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig1_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>Taste is defined as the detection of soluble compounds and is mediated by eight pairs of neurons (ADF, ADL, ASE, ASG, ASH, ASI, ASJ, ASK), while smell is defined as the detection of volatile compounds and is mediated by a separate set of three pairs of neurons (AWA, AWB, AWC) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4">4</xref>]. Despite its seemingly simple neural circuitry, <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> has the ability to discriminate between and respond to different chemical stimuli based on its previous experiences [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. In essence, <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> can learn and form memories from chemosensory data.</p><p>Through the use of chemotaxis assays, hundreds of aqueous and volatile chemicals have been identified as either attractants or repellants to <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>. This ability to discriminate between attractants and repellents is essential in order for <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> to successfully navigate its soil habitat in terms of both feeding behavior and spatial orientation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6">6</xref>]. Further genetic investigations into the behavior of <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> have lead to the discovery of a group of 14 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_7 subunits that are specifically involved in mediating chemotactic behavior [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6">6</xref>]. Future comparisons of the physical structure and biochemical action of these G-protein subunits and other signaling components will help to provide an even more detailed description of the chemosensory system and chemotactic behaviors of <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>.</p><p>A worm that is exposed to a taste or an odor for a long period of time decreases its response to the compound; this reversible decrease in response is called 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6">6</xref>]. In <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>, olfactory adaptation to different volatile compounds is mediated by either AWA or AWC sensory neurons. When a worm is adapted to a particular odorant, the responses to other odors detected by the same sensory neuron are not affected indicating that adaptation is not a cell wide phenomenon, but rather is odorant specific. Mutations in two genes, <italic toggle="yes">adp-1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">osm-,9</italic> expressed in the AWC sensory neurons, show normal initial responses to specific odors, however they fail to adapt to these odors [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6">6</xref>]. This suggests that detection of odors and adaptation to the odors are separate processes. The expression of adaptation differs depending on whether worms are in the presence of food or not. Thus, olfactory adaptation is another complex form of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_2 that can be studied in this simple system.</p></sec><sec id="Sec7"><title>Lower Level Process: Thermotaxis</title><p>As early as 1975, <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> was observed to show a behavioral response to thermal gradients [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7">7</xref>]. When <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> are cultivated in a well-fed state at a given temperature and then transferred to an environment containing a thermal gradient they will migrate to 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_9 equivalent to the temperature in which they were raised (Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2</xref>).<fig id="Fig2" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>C. elegans Neuroethology. Figure 2</label><caption><p>Path of a <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> on an agar filled Petri dish with a radial thermal gradient of 15–25˚C after being well fed at 20˚C. Wild-type (N2) strain shows thermotactic behavior (a) Mutant strains, or laser-ablated wild-types can be abnormal showing cryophilic (b) thermophilic (c) or athermotactic behavior (d).</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e2711" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig2_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig2_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 29093?><?image-md5 a2e3eb2b829bdd4a769e46961d73da45?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 110?><?image-original-width 480?><?image-scaled-height 110?><?image-scaled-width 480?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/a2e3eb2b829b/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig2_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig2_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 7184?><?thumb-md5 e4757626e402ca0af11024f957b332ab?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 46?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/e4757626e402/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig2_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>In contrast, worms experiencing starvation at a given temperature will avoid that temperature. This behavior appears to be the result of associative learning, where the worm learns to associate a specific temperature with the presence or absence of food.</p><p>In order for <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> to perform thermotaxis, they must be able to sense temperature. Laser ablation of any of the AFD, AIY, AIZ, and RIA neurons leads to animals with disrupted thermotactic behavior [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. It is believed that the actual sensation of temperature is accomplished by AFD sensory neurons, whose specialized 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13-like nerve endings are embedded just within the cuticle of the amphid sensillum in the nose of the worm [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. The axon projects from the amphid towards the AIY, AIZ, and RIA interneurons in the nerve ring in the neck area of the worm [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2">2</xref>]. Ablation of AIY or AIZ causes different abnormal behaviors, with <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> becoming either <xref rid="Sec1762" ref-type="sec">cryophilic</xref> or 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_20, respectively, while killing RIA leaves worms unable to track temperatures (athermotactic). Mori and colleagues [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>] have suggested that AIY and AIZ are interneurons integrated via direct synapses with the downstream interneuron RIA in order to produce the observed thermotactic response. When AFD neurons are destroyed using laser ablation, most but not all thermotactic behavior is arrested, indicating that there may be other neurons that have the ability to sense temperature; however, it is believed that most thermal information is collected by AFD [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>].</p><p>Studies of mutants showing abnormal thermotactic behavior lead to the discovery of components that may be involved in the cellular mechanisms of thermotaxis. <italic toggle="yes">tax-2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">tax-4</italic> are two genes that encode subunits of a <xref rid="Sec1844" ref-type="sec">cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channel</xref>. Mutants with disruptions of either <italic toggle="yes">tax-2</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">tax-4</italic> are athermotactic, completely ignoring thermal gradients [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. When the gene products of <italic toggle="yes">tax-2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">tax-4</italic> are tagged with 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_7, they are found localized to the membranes of the microvillus-like projections of AFD, suggesting an early role in the thermosensation mechanism [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. Interestingly, the hypothesized TAX-2/TAX-4 channel is most similar to the cGMP-gated channels found in rod photoreceptors of the human retina that are important for visual sensation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>].</p><p>Thermotactic behavior in <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> has become model of learning and memory because worms are able to learn and remember a specific temperature and pair this memory with the appropriate feeding-state [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>]. This memory can be modified simply by further cultivation for 2–4 h at a new temperature [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7">7</xref>]. Recently, mutants have been discovered that can memorize a cultivation temperature but cannot couple it to a feeding state [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5">5</xref>], suggesting that these processes are two distinct mechanisms.</p></sec><sec id="Sec8"><title>Lower Level Process: Mechanosensory Behavior</title><p>
<italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> responds to mechanosensory stimuli, in response to a touch to the head worms will swim backwards, in response to a touch to the tail worms will swim forwards. In addition, worms will swim backwards in response to a mechanical tap to their surroundings, such as within a laboratory Petri dish [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. This tap-withdrawal response is a perfect example of how a seemingly simple behavior has more complexity than it originally appears; this response is plastic and shows short-term 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8 and dishabituation, <xref rid="Sec1517" ref-type="sec">context conditioning</xref> and long-term memory for habituation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. Short-term habituation occurs with a series of taps separated by an inter-stimulus interval (ISI). Short ISIs lead to fast decreases in the withdrawal response, but this response is recovered quickly. Worms exposed to long ISIs, on the other hand, take longer to fully habituate, but have a much longer recovery period [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. The tap-withdrawal response can also show long-term memory of habituation lasting at least 24 h [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. The neural circuit for the tap response consists of the mechanosensory neurons ALM, AVM and PLM and the interneurons AVA, AVB, AVD and PVC [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. Behavioral experiments led to the hypothesis that plasticity was occurring at the synapse between the sensory neurons and interneurons [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. This synapse uses glutamate as its neurotransmitter, thus mutations that affect glutamate transmission affect both short-term and long-term memory. Mutations in the gene <italic toggle="yes">eat-4</italic>, which is responsible for expressing a pre-synaptic vesicular glutamate transporter, causes more rapid and complete short-term habituation of the tap-withdrawal response and no dishabituation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8">8</xref>]. When <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> have mutations in the gene, (<italic toggle="yes">glr-1</italic>) a post-synaptic glutamate receptor, no long-term memory of habituation is observed [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9">9</xref>]. This indicates that glutamate transmission between mechanosensory neurons and interneurons is necessary for short-term and long-term memory for habituation of the tap-withdrawal response in <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>. This is of special interest because glutamate transmission has been implicated in long-term memory in many different animals [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9">9</xref>], and may be part of a primitive, highly conserved mechanism of memory.</p></sec><sec id="Sec9"><title>Higher Level Process: Natural Variation in Feeding Behavior</title><p>Natural variations in feeding behavior have been identified within <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> populations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10">10</xref>]. Wild type (N2) strains feed in a solitary fashion, they slow down when they contact food, and disperse randomly as they feed. <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> variants such as the RC301 strain and <italic toggle="yes">npr-1</italic> mutants show a feeding pattern whereby they forage for food in groups, they speed up when they contact food and they congregate at the edges of food patches where levels of oxygen are low [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10">10</xref>]. The differences between the solitary and social strains are the result of a single amino acid substitution in the gene <italic toggle="yes">npr</italic>-1 (a predicted G protein-coupled receptor of the neuropeptide Y receptor family). The <italic toggle="yes">npr-1</italic> gene is expressed in several neurons (AQR, PQR and URX) that are exposed to <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> body fluid, and are involved in monitoring oxygen levels [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10">10</xref>]. This research demonstrates how a “social” behavior can be dissected genetically, allowing a deeper understanding of the ways that neurons can produce and regulate behavior.</p></sec><sec id="Sec10"><title>Summary</title><p>Detailed behavioral studies of the worm have shown that this tiny creature has a rich and complex behavioral repertoire, making it an ideal system in which to unravel the mysteries of the cellular control of behavior. Findings such as those described here contribute to the ever-growing database of knowledge within the <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> community. This database of knowledge (much of it available via the internet), coupled with the development of new investigative techniques, allows for research to be conducted at the behavioral, neuronal and genetic level making <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> an ideal model for the study of how genes regulate behavior.</p><p>Each of the examples that we have described show some of the ways that having all of the neurons in the nervous system identified and knowing their connectivity, as well as having a fully mapped and sequenced genome, has greatly aided the investigations of the roles of identified genes in behavior and extended our understanding of the neuroethology of <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec11"><title>C Fiber</title><sec id="Sec12"><title>Definition</title><p>The C fiber is an unmyelinated axon (less than 1 µm in diameter) found in a peripheral nerve trunk. It conducts pain and temperature senses.</p><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_4
</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec13"><title>C1 - C2 Cell Groups (Adrenergic Cell Groups)</title><sec id="Sec14"><title>Definition</title><p>The C1-C2 (and C3) cell groups are adrenergic cells groups located in the medulla. They contain the enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine. Projections to several regions have been found: paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus; locus coeruleus; solitary nucleus; dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus; and intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec15"><title>Ca<sup>2+</sup></title><sec id="Sec16"><title>Definition</title><p>The divalent calcium ion. </p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec29"><title>Cable Theory</title><sec id="Sec30"><title>Definition</title><p>Voltage signals in neurons travel down thin, long, cable-like dendritic and axonal processes. The theoretical modeling and mathematical/computational analysis of signal propagation within these processes is called cable theory. Due to the initial important work of Rall (see [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11">1</xref>] and references therein), much of the focus has been concerned with the effects of synaptic inputs propagating to the cell’s soma, how these inputs interact with each other, and how inputs to various dendritic tree locations affect the neuron’s output signal.</p></sec><sec id="Sec31"><title>Characteristics</title><p>Modeling various observed neural properties, where variations of voltage with location are important, leads to a partial differential equation description of the evolution of electrical potential in the neuron. For understanding information processing in neural networks, the contributions of individual neurons and their dendritic trees takes on central importance.</p><p>In the core conductor model of a neural process, cable theory classically has assumed a cylindrical membrane with an electrically conducting core. The core cross-section is sufficiently small compared to the length of the fiber that the core can be considered as cross-sectionally isopotential. Thus, the cable model only depends on voltage differences in the axial direction. The cell membrane is surrounded by extracellular space that is assumed isopotential. If the cable has physical length <italic toggle="yes">L</italic> (electrotonic length <italic toggle="yes">L/λ)</italic>, then a reasonable boundary condition at <italic toggle="yes">x = L</italic> is to have zero axial current. With longitudinal current being proportional to the spatial derivative of potential, this (“sealed-end”) boundary condition just states that this spatial derivative of <italic toggle="yes">v</italic> equals zero at <italic toggle="yes">x = L</italic>, for all time <italic toggle="yes">t > 0</italic>. Then the left-end (somatic) boundary condition is a linear combination of potential and its space and time rates of change at <italic toggle="yes">x = 0</italic>. See [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14">4</xref>] for details.</p></sec><sec id="Sec33"><title>Passive Dendritic Trees and Rall’s Equivalent Cylinder Theorem</title><p>In the motoneuron model above the dendritic structure is represented by a single cylinder. Under certain constraints a branching structure can be reduced to a single electrically equivalent cylinder model [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR13">3</xref>]. This approach has proved quite useful in interpreting various experimental observations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11">1</xref>]. The structure Rall set up is flexible enough to handle arbitrary branching geometries where the branches may have nonuniform membrane properties.</p><p>To give some idea of the assumptions needed (consult [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12">2</xref>] for details) consider first a simple tree with a “trunk” segment connected to a soma (at <italic toggle="yes">x = 0</italic>), and at each branch point of the tree there is a parent branch (with radius <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>
<sub><italic toggle="yes">parent</italic></sub> in the direction of the soma, and some number of sibling branches emanating from it. Some assumptions imposed on the tree are: the initial depolarization is the same at all points equal distance from the soma (for instance, the whole tree is at its rest potential), and each dendritic tip has the same terminal boundary condition (e.g., the sealed-end condition). Also, at each branching point a three-halves law is assumed to hold: <inline-formula id="IEq16"><tex-math id="M18"><?equation-image-name M18.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 15cc6bad9a2471a5690c73823d48d139?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/15cc6bad9a24/M18.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

$$(a_{parent} )^{3/2} = \sum\nolimits_i {a_i ^{3/2} },$$
\end{document}</tex-math></inline-formula> the sum taken over all sibling branches <italic toggle="yes">i</italic> associated with the specific parent branch. This can be considered an 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_9 matching condition, and it is a reasonable physiological approximation in many cases [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR13">3</xref>]. Rall had the assumption that with distances measured in space constants <italic toggle="yes">λ</italic>, the dendritic terminal points were assumed to be at the same electrotonic distance from the soma. This is generally not satisfied; dendritic tips can vary considerably across branches. This may have the effect that an equivalent cylinder actually tapers gradually to zero moving from the soma to its terminus. However, the assumption has been weakened in later generalizations of the theory. With these conditions the depolarization at any point in the tree can be determined from the solution to the cable equation at the same distance from the soma.</p><p>There are relatively few problems of interest that can be solved analytically and so one must resort to numerical methods. Because of morphological complexity of dendritic trees and the need to investigate the effects of distributed synaptic inputs, there are now excellent modeling simulation tools available that take the philosophy that cables and trees can be segmented into numerous compartments.</p></sec><sec id="Sec34"><title>Nonlinear Cable Theory</title><p>If the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13 is not relatively close to the neuron’s rest potential, and the cable has active ion channels, then the current-voltage relation <italic toggle="yes">i</italic>
<sub><italic toggle="yes">ion</italic></sub> in (<xref rid="Equ1" ref-type="">1</xref>) has nonlinear dependence on voltage. The most important and most studied example of this is the Hodgkin–Huxley model [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR16">6</xref>]. The Hodgkin-Huxley model for squid giant axon could reproduce and explain a large range of data, including shape and <xref rid="Sec1437" ref-type="sec">conduction velocity</xref> of a propagating action potential (impulse), its sharp threshold, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_18, anode-break excitation, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1, and subthreshold oscillations. The conductance-based modeling framework formulated by the Hodgkin-Huxley model has remained remarkably flexible for modeling other neural processes, including some human neuronal processes.</p><p>Much of the analysis of the cable model of Hodgkin and Huxley (including later modifications, generalizations, and simplifications) has concerned the initiation and behavior of single impulses and pulse trains under various circumstances. Examples include dependence of conduction speed on temperature, density of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19, conductance properties, initiation and sustained firing patterns, etc. (see, e.g. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15">5</xref>]).</p><p>Dendrites (and axons) are very non-uniform, particularly in geometry and distribution of ionic channels. Generalizations of classical cable theory have tried to assess a functional role for these non-uniformities, taking into consideration the cell type, but results are rather scattered. The effect on conduction when there are present significant changes in dendritic cable diameter has had a long history. The main issues here concern conditions for conduction block (stopping spike propagation), and reflecting “echo” waves that back propagate [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR17">7</xref>]. This behavior may have functional consequences regarding synaptic activity. Also, the distribution of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_4 on a cable can determine whether signal propagation will be successful. Simulations show that sometimes clumping of spines is needed for successful conduction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18">8</xref>]. As an example of another study, model simulations of a cable show amplification of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5even when there are only persistent sodium channels that are sparsely distributed in isolated clumps [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19">9</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec35"><title>Myelinated Cable Modeling</title><p>The most extreme non-uniform case is that of myelinated (myelination) axons. Because sodium channels are concentrated at 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14, and various ion channels are in relatively low density in the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_9, theoretical models have concentrated on saltatory aspects of conduction (salutatory conduction), and have incorporated spatially discrete dynamics. These models assumed the internodes were perfect insulators. Cable theory based models have considered the internodes as passive cable segments, separated by active nodes (see, e.g. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12">2</xref>]). Simulations have indicated that internodal structure and parameters have far more control on velocity than does the node, though the nodal characteristics are important for getting the correct threshold level. Analysis and simulation studies have most often been concerned with the dependence of conduction velocity on parameters such as diameter ratio between node and internode, internodal length, temperature, ratio of capacitances, etc. For example, if the internodal length and internodal diameter (with 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13) is, respectively, L and D, and d is the axon diameter, then conduction velocity tends to be insensitive to d/D and L/D over a range of values, and tending to increase linearly with d, other parameters being fixed. Where investigated, conduction will proceed through one unexcitable node, but if there are two adjacent unexcitable nodes conduction block will generally occur. Some studies have looked at the effects of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_4 and partial remyelination on conduction characteristics. For example, Waxman and Brill [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20">10</xref>] studied conduction near demyelinated regions. The reduction in length of two internodes closest to the demyelinated regions to approximately one third of their normal length or less will still facilitate conduction.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec36"><title>CaCC</title><sec id="Sec37"><title>Definition</title><p>

</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec47"><title>Cadherins</title><sec id="Sec48"><title>Synonyms</title><p>Cadherin superfamily</p></sec><sec id="Sec49"><title>Definition</title><p>Founding members of the cadherin superfamily were identified by their ability to mediate calcium-dependent cell-to-cell adhesion. They were designated as cadherins (<italic toggle="yes">ca</italic>lcium + <italic toggle="yes">adher</italic>e + prote<italic toggle="yes">in</italic>) and are now classified as classical cadherins. Classical cadherins are type I transmembrane proteins and defined by two additional structural features (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">1</xref>). One is the extracellular cadherin repeat or cadherin domain of roughly 110 amino acids, which mediates calcium-dependent homotypic interaction between cells. This domain is typically organized in tandem repeats. Another is the intracellular domain with which a group of cytoplasmic molecules, i.e., catenins, interact. In addition to classical cadherins, the cadherin superfamily includes many subfamilies of non-classical cadherins [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>]. Although non-classical molecules also have cadherin repeats in their ectodomains, they lack the catenin-binding motif and are characterized by a variety of transmembrane domains and intracellular sequences. Non-classical cadherins include desmosomal cadherins, protocadherins and seven-pass transmembrane cadherins. “Cadherin” is used as a synonym for classical cadherin hereafter.<fig id="Fig5" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Cadherins. Figure 1</label><caption><p>Structural diversity of the cadherin superfamily. Overall structures of four selected members of the cadherin superfamily: a vertebrate classical cadherin (about 750 amino acids in length), two <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> classic cadherins (<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>E and <italic toggle="yes">D</italic>N are 1,507 and 3,108 respectively) and the <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> seven-pass transmembrane cadherin, Flamingo (3,575). Both vertebrate and <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> classical cadherins have catenin-binding domains, although the number of repeats and the presence or absence of other extracellular motifs are variable.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e4094" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig5_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig5_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 56338?><?image-md5 b01e6006e79c40c48b3f6d13e1aa937a?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 314?><?image-original-width 354?><?image-scaled-height 314?><?image-scaled-width 354?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/b01e6006e79c/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig5_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig5_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 15441?><?thumb-md5 12a46c3d404a28476dd7f4e81263cfa5?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 89?><?thumb-scaled-width 100?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/12a46c3d404a/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig5_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p></sec><sec id="Sec50"><title>Characteristics</title><sec id="Sec51"><title>Quantitative Description</title><p>In a single vertebrate species such as humans, over 20 different subtypes of classical cadherins have been found so far, whereas the total number of non-classical cadherins is 80 at a moderate estimate.</p></sec><sec id="Sec52"><title>Description of the Structures</title><p>Each vertebrate classical cadherin has five cadherin repeats, whereas the number of repeats and the presence or absence of other extracellular motifs are variable among invertebrate cadherins [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>], even in a single species such as <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> (Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">1</xref>).</p><p>Compared to other cell-surface molecules, such as calcium-independent cell adhesion molecules, cadherins are unique in their ability to induce tight cell aggregates in which cells adhere to neighbors with maximum areas of contact. This ability appears to be dependent on the interaction of the cadherin–catenin multiprotein complex with the actin cytoskeleton. The classification of non-classical cadherins is based on sequence similarities of their intracellular regions and the overall structure of all domains. It is reasonable to assume that distinct subfamilies of non-classical cadherins are responsible for different functions and that they are coupled to different signaling pathways that have been under investigation.</p></sec><sec id="Sec53"><title>Higher Level Structures and Their Regulation</title><sec id="Sec54"><title>3D Structure of Ectodomains</title><p>In the presence of calcium, cells expressing a certain subtype of classical cadherins only form stable contacts with cells expressing the same type, with some exceptions. This homotypic adhesion between cells arises from homophilic interactions between ectodomains of the same subtype and consequently differential expression of cadherins underlies various roles in vivo (as explained later). Many different structural approaches have been used to unravel the molecular basis for cadherin-mediate adhesion. Although several different models of the cadherin homophilic bond have been proposed, all essentially agree that the specificity lies in the most N-terminal part of the ectodomains and that molecular interaction occurs not only between adjacent cells (in trans), but also on the surface of the same cell (in cis) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR23">3</xref>]. A study using a two-repeat fragment of E-cadherin showed that calcium-binding in between consecutive repeats stabilizes otherwise flexible linker regions.</p></sec><sec id="Sec55"><title>Distinct Protein Complexes at Two Intercellular Junctions</title><p>Classical cadherins, one subfamily of non-classical cadherins (desmosomal cadherins) and their associated proteins are structural components of intercellular junctions that were previously documented at the electron microscopic level. In polarized epithelial cells, the adherens junction (AJ) is formed near the apical surface and E-cadherin is typically localized there [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR24">4</xref>]. Catenins assemble on the intracellular domain of E-cadherin and this complex is linked to the cortical actin. An AJ is not necessarily a stable structure. Epithelial cells regulate their contacts with neighboring cells during development and in disease states such as tumor metastasis. Underlying mechanisms include endocytic recycling of cadherin and loss of one of the catenins by mutations respectively [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR25">5</xref>]. A synapse contains cadherins and catenins and is structurally similar to an AJ (see below).</p><p>A desmosome is another type of intercellular junction that is abundant in tissues that experience mechanical stress, where two subtypes of desmosomal cadherins, desmocollins and desmogleins, are localized. Heterodimers of desmocollin and desmoglein are linked to the keratin intermediate filament cytoskeleton via interactions with one of the catenins, plakoglobin, and other components of the desmosome.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec56"><title>Function</title><sec id="Sec57"><title>Cell Sorting, Cell Rearrangement and Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transitions</title><p>Maintenance of solid tissues is just one of the multiple missions of classical cadherins. Differential expression of cadherin subtypes and spatiotemporal control of cadherin–catenin activity play pivotal roles in dynamic morphogenetic events that take place numerous times during development [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">6</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27">7</xref>]. Such tissue morphogenesis can be classified at least into three categories. First there are numerous examples demonstrating that cell populations expressing different cadherins sort out in vivo and boundaries are generated between them. For example, expression of N-cadherin in the presumptive neural epithelium allows it to separate from the E-cadherin-expressing ectoderm. Other examples are the roles of cadherins in the establishment/maintenance of early embryonic brain divisions. Second, dynamic breaking and reforming of cadherin adhesive cell–cell binding is required for cells to change neighbors and this cell rearrangement controls the reshaping of tissues. Third, epithelial cells are often converted to motile, fibroblast-like cells and a hallmark of this epithelial to mesenchymal transition is decreased expression of E-cadherin. Down-regulation or dysfunction of E-cadherin also plays a part in tumor cell invasion and metastasis.</p></sec><sec id="Sec58"><title>Axonal and Dendritic Outgrowth, Fasciculation, Pathfinding and Target Recognition</title><p>A number of classical cadherins are distributed in axons during the period of active elongation and the expression of most vertebrate cadherins studied to date is restricted to subsets of growing fiber tracts. It therefore has been assumed that cadherins are used by growth cones to navigate along pre-existing pathways expressing the same type of cadherin. A number of in vitro experiments indicate that N-cadherin is an excellent substrate for axonal outgrowth from N-cadherin-positive neurons and is also required for axonal fasciculation. Furthermore in vivo analyses have strengthened or demonstrated roles of cadherins in various aspects of neuronal network formation including axonal and dendritic outgrowth, fasciculation, pathfinding and target recognition [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27">7</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28">8</xref>].</p><p>In the Xenopus visual system, expression of a dominant negative form or injection of antibodies against N-cadherin cause loss or reduction of neurite growth or pathfinding errors. Genetic studies in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic> have shown that loss of N-cadherin function causes defective axonal fasciculation and pathfinding errors in mutant animals. In the fly visual system, N-cadherin appears to mediate a homophilic, attractive interaction between photoreceptor growth cones and their targets that precedes synaptic partner choice. An important role of cadherin in dendrodendritic interaction is shown in the fly olfactory system. N-cadherin confines dendritic terminals of projection neurons (counterparts of vertebrate mitral cells) to a particular glomerulus following an initial overgrowth into adjacent glomeruli.</p><p>Non-classical cadherins also regulate neuronal wiring; for example a series of recent studies have revealed that seven-pass transmembrane cadherins are involved in regulation of dendritic growth. The <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> seven-pass transmembrane cadherin Flamingo (Fmi; also known as Starry night) is required for sensory neurons and central mushroom-body neurons to restrict dendritic growth. In contrast to the overextension phenotypes in the fly nervous system, knockdown of one of the mammalian Fmi homologs, Celsr2, by a RNA interference (RNAi) approach in pyramidal and Purkinje neurons reduced branch number and length, leading to simplification of dendritic arbors. What the downstream signal transduction pathways are and why loss of Fmi function and knocking down of Celsr2 produce superficially opposite phenotypes are under investigation. Another vertebrate homolog, Celsr3, is required for formation of major axonal fascicles in the mouse brain.</p></sec><sec id="Sec59"><title>Synaptogenesis and Synaptic Plasticity</title><p>After axons traverse long distances and reach correct target regions, these axons and the dendritic filopodia of their target cells recognize each other and subsequently form a synapse. Neurons utilize the characteristics of classical cadherins to “zip synapses up.” Classical cadherins are detected at the earliest points of axon-filopodial contact and persist in mature synapses where cadherins and catenins are localized in the close vicinity of the transmitter-release zone, although this varies according to the type of synapse. Roles of cadherins and catenins in synapse formation have been examined in cultured mammalian neurons and in the visual system of <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> mutants. These studies have indicated that the cadherin–catenin system is required for stabilizing contacts between incoming axons and targets, morphological maturation of synapse and the maintenance of stable synaptic contacts through regulating spine motility [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27">7</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28">8</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29">9</xref>]. A sub-class of protocadherins, protocadherin γ, is also found in synaptic junctions.</p><p>Multiple subtypes of classical cadherins are expressed in the brain and their expression profiles often correlate with neuronal connectivity. This finding, together with the homophilic binding specificity of individual subtypes, led to the proposal that the differential binding among the subtypes may connect pre- and post-synaptic membranes and lock them together, thus forming selective neuronal connections. Many protocadherins are also expressed in the nervous system. Thus it is intriguing to envisage whether the molecular diversity of classic cadherins and protocadherins play a role in specifying synaptic connectivity and if so, how the roles of these two different subfamilies came to be differentiated.</p><p>Cadherins are also important physiologically. Application of anti-N-cadherin antibodies to hippocampal slices indicated that N-cadherin is needed to hold nascent synaptic contacts and establish L-LTP. The functions of cadherins and catenins have been studied at the behavioral level as well. For example, LTP is elevated in hippocampal neurons in cadherin-11-knockout mice. This observation has been explained by assuming that reducing the activity of cadherin might enhance the deformability of spines, so rendering them more sensitive to LTP-inducing stimuli.</p></sec><sec id="Sec60"><title>Planar Cell Polarity</title><p>In many organs, epithelial cells are polarized not only along the apicobasal axis, but also along a second axis within a plane. Acquisition of the latter polarity, known as planar cell polarity (PCP) or tissue polarity, is crucial for specialized cellular functions. A typical example of PCP is seen in the sensory epithelium of the inner ear, where stereocilia that protrude from the apical surfaces of hair cells are uniformly oriented. This coordinated alignment maximizes the ear’s sensitivity to sound and acceleration. Genetic programming of PCP has been thoroughly studied in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic>. Such studies highlight the pivotal roles of three non-classic cadherins, the seven-pass transmembrane cadherin Flamingo (Fmi) and the single-pass transmembrane proteins Dachsous (Ds) and Fat (Ft) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR30">10</xref>]. It was previously postulated that polarity information is passed from one end of a tissue to another, possibly via a secreted factor; nowadays it is speculated that direct cell–cell interaction, mediated by Ds–Ft heterophilic interaction, transmits polarity locally within the tissue and that subsequently Fmi is involved in polarization of individual cells. All of the three <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> molecules are conserved in vertebrates and at least one of the Flamingo homologs has been shown to be required for acquisition of PCP in the mouse inner ear.</p></sec></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec61"><title>Cadmium-insensitive Pacemakers</title><sec id="Sec62"><title>Definition</title><p>Pacemaker neurons that are dependent on persistent sodium (Na<sup>+</sup>) current and burst in the presence of cadmium.</p><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_16
