</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec63"><title>Cadmium-sensitive Pacemakers</title><sec id="Sec64"><title>Definition</title><p>Pacemaker neurons that depend on calcium-activated non-specific cation (CAN) current and are blocked by cadmium.</p><p>
<xref rid="Sec67" ref-type="sec">Calcium-activated Non-specific Cation (CAN) Current</xref>
</p><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_18
</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec65"><title>Calcitonin Gene Related Peptide (CGRP)</title><sec id="Sec66"><title>Definition</title><p>CGRP is one of the numerous peptides found in neurons and acting as co-transmitters. It is derived from the gene encoding calcitonin by alternative splicing of mRNA and by proteolytic processing of a precursor peptide. It is mainly found in sensory neurons of the central nervous system. Its prime target is the CGRP receptor, a member of the family of G protein-coupled receptors. In contrast to calcitonin, which is involved in calcium homeostasis and bone remodelling, CGRP causes vasodilatation and vascular leakage. It is expressed in group C sensory nerve fibers. It works as a stimulatory (pro-nociceptive) neurotransmitter when it is released centrally, and as a pro-inflammatory mediator when released peripherally. The central role of CGRP in primary headaches has led to a search for suitable antagonists of CGRP receptors.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec67"><title>Calcium-activated Non-specific Cation (CAN) Current</title><sec id="Sec68"><title>Definition</title><p>An inward current that is generated by ion channels that open in response to an increased intracellular calcium concentration. The opening of these ion channels leads to an inward current that is carried by non-specific cations including calcium and sodium ions. The CAN current has been implicated in generating pacemaker activity in various pacemaker neuron types.</p><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_2
</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec69"><title>Calcium Binding Proteins</title><sec id="Sec70"><title>Synonyms</title><p>Syt; 65-kDa synaptic vesicle protein; CaMKII; Type II Ca/Calmodulin-dependent kinase</p></sec><sec id="Sec71"><title>Definition</title><p>Syt: A putative major Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for synaptic transmission, which resides in the synaptic vesicle membrane. Syt has two Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding domains (<xref rid="Sec108" ref-type="sec">Calcium domain</xref>) and binds multiple Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions.</p><p>CaMKII: A major constituent of Postsynaptic density in excitatory synapses in the mammalian brain.</p></sec><sec id="Sec72"><title>Characteristics</title><p>Ca<sup>2+</sup> is a ubiquitous messenger and participates in a variety of cell functions in physiological and pathological conditions. The specificity of signal transmission is maintained by spatial and temporal localization of Ca<sup>2+</sup> signals and Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding proteins. At the synapse, Ca<sup>2+</sup> plays crucial roles both in pre- and post-synaptic events. In each event, specialized Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding proteins are involved. Among Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding proteins at the synapse two proteins have been extensively studied. The role of a Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding protein in the presynaptic terminal (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1), Synaptotagmin (Syt), is generally believed to be in detection of Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx for synchronized fusion of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 (for review, [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR31">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32">2</xref>]). Another Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding protein, Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) is abundant in the postsynaptic membrane and essential for plastic regulation of glutamate receptor channels (for review, [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33">3</xref>]). There are many other Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding proteins in neurons. Calbindin-D28K, calretinin and parvalbumin are distributed in specific neurons in the brain and considered to play a role as Ca<sup>2+</sup> buffers. Calmodulin modifies channel functions and neuronal excitability, whereas Protein kinase C is involved in modulation of glutamate receptor channel functions and synaptic plasticity in the brain. Annexins are a family of Ca<sup>2+</sup>- and phospholipid-binding proteins and bind to various presynaptic proteins such as rabphilin and synapsin. CAPS, Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent activator protein for secretion, is an essential cytosolic component of the protein machinery involved in large dense-core vesicle exocytosis and in secretion of a subset of neurotransmitters.</p><p>In this essay, concentration will be on Syt in the presynaptic nerve terminal and CaMKII in the postsynaptic cell.</p><sec id="Sec73"><title>Synaptotagmin (Syt)</title><p>Electrical signals conveyed along an axon are converted into chemical signals at the synapse. The basic mechanism for synaptic transmission was established at the frog neuromuscular junction, about 50 years ago, by Katz and his collaborators [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34">4</xref>]. Ca<sup>2+</sup> plays the central role in this story. The electrical signal at the presynaptic terminal results in a transient influx of Ca<sup>2+</sup> through voltage-gated Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels, which is detected by a specialized Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor. Through a series of molecular interactions, this signal causes rapid fusion of synaptic vesicles and transmitter release. Among Ca<sup>2+</sup> -binding proteins in the presynaptic terminal, Syt is the most promising candidate for the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor.</p></sec><sec id="Sec74"><title>Ca/Calmodulin-Dependent Protein Kinase II (CaMKII)</title><p>Synaptic transmission is malleable and plastic, which is believed to be the basis for memory and learning. Ca<sup>2+</sup> again plays an important role in this process. CaMKII is the major player among Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding proteins in the postsynaptic side of the synapse. This kinase has been studied extensively in the mammalian central nervous system as it constitutes the postsynaptic density, and is intimately involved in 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12 of synaptic transmission in the brain.</p></sec><sec id="Sec75"><title>Quantitative Description</title><sec id="Sec76"><title>Molecular Weight</title><p>Syt: ~65 kDa, probably works as an oligomer.</p><p>CaMKII, CaMKIIα, ~50 kDa and CaMKIIβ, ~60 kDa: Carboxy-terminal holoenzymes consisting of a stacked pair of hexameric subunit rings [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR35">5</xref>].</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec77"><title>Higher Level Structures</title><p>Syt; Neurons, Endocrine and Exocrine cells, Presynaptic terminals, Synaptic vesicles, CaMKII; Mammalian brain, Hippocampus, Neurons, Synapses.</p></sec><sec id="Sec78"><title>Lower Level Components</title><p>Syt: A major protein in the membrane of synaptic vesicles and dense core vesicles, which has an amino (N)-terminal transmembrane region followed by two C<sub>2</sub> domains (C2A and C2B). The C<sub>2</sub> domains are in the cytoplasm and uniquely situated to sense Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx at the transmitter release site.</p><p>CaMKII: A major component in the postsynaptic density in the glutamatergic synapse.</p></sec><sec id="Sec79"><title>Homologs</title><p>Syt: Syt includes 13 isoforms in humans, and by the database search, an additional six potential isoforms have been suggested. Although most Syt’s are localized on transport vesicles, some (Syt III, VI, and VII) are present at the plasma membrane.</p><p>CaMKII, CaMKIIα, and CaMKIIβ are major isoforms in the brain.</p></sec><sec id="Sec80"><title>Higher Level Processes</title><p>Syt: Inter-neuronal communication, regulation of hormone secretion.</p><p>CaMKII: Postsynaptic modulation of synaptic transmission, synaptic plasticity, memory and learning.</p></sec><sec id="Sec81"><title>Lower Level Processes</title><p>Syt: 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_22, transmitter release.</p><p>CaMKII: Regulation of channel permeability and insertion of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in the postsynaptic density.</p></sec><sec id="Sec82"><title>Process Regulation</title><p>CaMKII: Extensive synaptic activities translocate CaMKII from cytosol in the postsynaptic 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 of dendrites to the postsynaptic density.</p></sec><sec id="Sec83"><title>Function</title><sec id="Sec84"><title>Syt</title><sec id="Sec85"><title>Characteristics of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> Sensor for Fast Synaptic Transmission</title><p>The Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_6 has the following characteristics: Synaptic potentials are steeply dependent on the Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentration, indicating that multiple Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions have to bind to the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for fast synaptic transmission. Furthermore, Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for synaptic transmission is considered to have a low Ca<sup>2+</sup> affinity. In a microdomain, the Ca concentration is considered to increase rapidly to high levels, since slow binding EGTA does not affect synaptic transmission but fast BAPTA does (but see review by Augustine et al. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">6</xref>]). Since the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor detects transient changes (sub-msec) of Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentrations in the micro- or nano-domain, accurate determination of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentration has been difficult. Two methods are suitable to estimate local Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentrations. Caged Ca<sup>2+</sup> can be released instantaneously by photolysis. Since caged Ca<sup>2+</sup> compound can be equilibrated before photolysis, uncaged Ca<sup>2+</sup> will distribute homogeneously in the presynaptic nerve terminal, and the Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentration can be determined with a Ca<sup>2+</sup> dye injected together with the caged Ca<sup>2+</sup> compound. At the rat auditory synapse, calyx of Held, estimated values for release of transmitter are around 10 µM. Whereas, by using Ca<sup>2+</sup>-sensitive K<sup>+</sup> channels localized close to presynaptic Ca channels as a probe for local changes of Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentration, the peak concentration was estimated to be 175 µM (for review, [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">6</xref>]). Thus, the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for fast synaptic transmission has a relatively low affinity for Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Syt is localized close to the release site and has multiple binding sites with low Ca<sup>2+</sup> affinities. Thus, Syt is a good candidate for the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor.</p></sec><sec id="Sec86"><title>Functional Sites in Syt</title><p>Syt has multiple finding sides. Two Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding domains, C2A and C2B, altogether have five putative Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding sites. Among these binding sites, recent evidence indicates that C2B is the Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensing domain for fast synaptic transmission (Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">1</xref>; [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR37">7</xref>]).<fig id="Fig6" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Binding Proteins. Figure 1</label><caption><p>Structure of Synaptotagmin I. C2A and C2B domains are oriented with their Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding sites in a close proximity (reproduced from Fernandez et al. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR37">7</xref>] with permission).</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e4669" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig6_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig6_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 58960?><?image-md5 47fa6d232edf97ef1cccb083da79c5c1?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 197?><?image-original-width 354?><?image-scaled-height 197?><?image-scaled-width 354?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/47fa6d232edf/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig6_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig6_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 18409?><?thumb-md5 03955e1aa8a2983a9fb8ada6aab160d4?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 143?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/03955e1aa8a2/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig6_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p></sec><sec id="Sec87"><title>Oligomerization</title><p>Syt oligomerizes Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependently. Whether this oligomerization is essential for vesicle fusion is a current issue. Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent oligomerization occurs at C2B, and is conserved in all members of the Syt family.</p></sec><sec id="Sec88"><title>Phospholipid Binding</title><p>Syt binds phospholipids Ca<sup>2+</sup> dependently, and this interaction is proposed to be a trigger for vesicle fusion.</p></sec><sec id="Sec89"><title>Interaction with SNARE Complex</title><p>Syt also binds syntaxin 1, SNAP-25, Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels, and AP-2. AP-2 is an adaptor protein for clathrin that is essential for endocytosis (for review [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32">2</xref>]). Syt seems to be a multifunctional protein.</p></sec><sec id="Sec90"><title>Phenotypes of Syt I-Null Mutations</title><p>Animals that lack Syt were generated in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">C. elegans</italic>, and mouse. Synaptic transmission in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila syt I</italic>-null embryos, and in synapses formed in culture from neurons derived from <italic toggle="yes">syt I</italic>-null mouse embryos, have been studied. Nerve-evoked synchronous synaptic transmission is severely impaired, supporting the hypothesis that Syt I is a major Ca<sup>2+</sup> sensor for fast synaptic transmission [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32">2</xref>].</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec91"><title>CaMKII (CaMKIIα and CaMKIIβ)</title><sec id="Sec92"><title>Localization</title><p>The postsynaptic density (PSD), an electron-dense structure directly apposed to the cytoplasmic face of the postsynaptic membrane, is prominent at excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the mammalian brain. CaMKII is a major protein in the PSD, and is specifically localized to the cytoplasmic face of PSD in a single layer, and in a highly ordered array of tower-like structures (Fig. <xref rid="Fig7" ref-type="fig">2</xref>; [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38">8</xref>]).<fig id="Fig7" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Binding Proteins. Figure 2</label><caption><p>Diagram showing the structural relation between CaMKII and postsynaptic density (reproduced from Petersen et al. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38">8</xref>] with permission).</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e4750" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig7_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig7_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 68244?><?image-md5 ccce3c35cc6ba5c3764cbc953171f824?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 269?><?image-original-width 354?><?image-scaled-height 269?><?image-scaled-width 354?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/ccce3c35cc6b/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig7_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig7_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 17990?><?thumb-md5 62edf2ae20a38de0c3d6e5f71aaf4ef8?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 105?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/62edf2ae20a3/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig7_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>This location of CaMKII is highly suited for detection of Ca<sup>2+</sup> entering through NMDA-type glutamate receptor channels. CaMKII may be connected directly to 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14.</p></sec><sec id="Sec93"><title>Phosphorylation</title><p>CaMKIIα and CaMKIIβ are contained in relatively high concentrations in brain tissue and phosphorylate non-specifically Ser and Thr residues in numerous proteins. CaMKII binding to NMDA receptors exposes CaMKII to high Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentrations entering through the channels and induces autophosphorylation, which is necessary for induction of long-term potentiation (LTP). Once phosphorylated, CaMKII binds more tightly to the NMDA receptor channel and is persistently active, even after a fall in the Ca<sup>2+</sup> level. This persistent activity then promotes enzymatic and structural processes that increase the number of AMPA-type glutamate receptor channels in the postsynaptic membrane.</p></sec><sec id="Sec94"><title>Translocation During Synaptic Activities</title><p>Upon strong activation of NMDA receptor channels, CaMKII translocates to the PSD, where it can optimally detect Ca<sup>2+</sup> entry through NMDA receptor channels and become phosphorylated. Under this condition, more 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 are recruited into the PSD [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR39">9</xref>]. By interaction with CaMKII, AMPA receptor channels also increase the single channel conductance. Both of these effects lead to potentiation of AMPA-mediated synaptic transmission.</p></sec><sec id="Sec95"><title>Memory Impairments in CaMKII Knock-Out Mice</title><p>As described above, the involvement of CaMKII in LTP is convincing, however, it is yet to be established whether LTP is essential in memory acquisition in the animal. This was studied in CaMKIIα knock-out mice. In these mice, the hippocampus was deficient in LTP, although synaptic transmission was normal. These mice exhibit spatial learning impairments [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR40">10</xref>]. Thus, CaMKII plays an important role in the higher brain functions.</p></sec></sec></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec96"><title>Calcium/Calmodulin-dependent Protein Kinase ll in Neurons</title><sec id="Sec97"><title>Synonyms</title><p>CaM kinase II; CaMKII</p></sec><sec id="Sec98"><title>Definition</title><p>Calcium(Ca<sup>2+</sup>)/<xref rid="Sec135" ref-type="sec">calmodulin</xref>-dependent protein kinase II, or CaMKII, is a multifunctional serine-threonine 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_11 highly abundant in the brain (1–2% of all proteins). The enzyme is activated by the binding of the complex Ca<sup>2+</sup>-calmodulin (CaM). The hallmarks of CaMKII are its unique structural and regulatory properties, which endow the enzyme with the ability to decode the spatial and temporal patterns of Ca<sup>2+</sup> signals. As such, the enzyme is well equipped to control multiple functions in nerve cells via the ubiquitous Ca<sup>2+</sup> signaling systems. CaMKII is particularly abundant in the post-synaptic density (PSD), accounting for its important role in synaptic plasticity and some forms of learning and memory. This essay is an overview of the structure and regulation of CaMKII followed by some examples of how the unique features of the enzyme support its ability to serve as a major decoder of neuronal activity. Finally, a particular focus is made on the important role of CaMKII in regulating glutamatergic synapses of the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8, because, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 and the implication of CaMKII have been extensively studied in this brain region.</p></sec><sec id="Sec99"><title>Characteristics</title><sec id="Sec100"><title>Structure and Regulation of CaMKII</title><p>The CaMKII family is encoded by four different genes α, β, δ and γ, from which at least 28 isoforms can be derived. The gene encodes for three principal domains in the protein: catalytic, autoinhibitory and association domains. In the brain, the α and β genes are predominantly expressed. In the cell, the enzyme is not expressed as a single protein, but rather as a homo- or heteromeric complex (holoenzyme) of 12 subunits. The 12 catalytic and regulatory domains form 2 hexameric rings on each side of a central core comprising 12 association domains (Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">1</xref>).<fig id="Fig8" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium/Calmodulin-dependent Protein Kinase ll in Neurons. Figure 1</label><caption><p>Structure of CaMKII. (a) Primary structure of CaMKII domains. (b) Model structure of CaMKII dodecamer. (c) Model of CaMKII activation by Ca<sup>2+</sup> spikes [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">3</xref>].</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e4873" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig8_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig8_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 86030?><?image-md5 6a047024570a70e35143807b15a37895?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 471?><?image-original-width 480?><?image-scaled-height 471?><?image-scaled-width 480?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/6a047024570a/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig8_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig8_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 10317?><?thumb-md5 c26ffad68c66a1cb076b7b9483b625ab?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 98?><?thumb-scaled-width 100?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/c26ffad68c66/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig8_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>The catalytic domain is not only responsible for substrate phosphorylation, it also supports the binding of the enzyme to various proteins. Under basal conditions, the autoinhibitory domain keeps its counterpart catalytic domain inactive [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">3</xref>]. The structure of both the catalytic and regulatory domains of CaMKII, in its autoinhibited conformation, has been recently determined by crystallography, revealing that the regulatory segments of two subunits form a dimeric structure that blocks 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 and substrate binding to the catalytic domain [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">3</xref>]. Following a rise in intracellular Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>-bound CaM (Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM) molecules bind to the autoinhibitory domain of individual kinase subunits thereby activating them by relieving their inhibition.</p><sec id="Sec101"><title>CaMKII as a Molecular Memory</title><p>CaMKII activity is regulated by Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM binding, but also by phosphorylation. Binding of Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM not only activates each kinase subunit, but also exposes an important amino acid for their regulation: Thr286 (for α isoforms, Thr287 for β isoforms). This amino acid on one subunit can be phosphorylated by a neighboring catalytic domain from another subunit in the holoenzyme, a process termed autophosphorylation. Autophosphorylation at Thr286, residing in the autoinhibitory domain, switches the kinase subunit to an autonomous, Ca<sup>2+</sup>-independent state. Thus, once Ca<sup>2+</sup> levels in the cell have returned to baseline, the phosphorylated subunits remain active despite the eventual dissociation of Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM, which itself is also slowed down 10,000 fold. As such, Thr286 phosphorylation is considered a biochemical memory of a previous rise in Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Following Thr286 phosphorylation and Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM dissociation, a second autophosphorylation can occur at Thr305/306, located in the Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM binding domain. But in opposition to Thr286, this phosphorylation blocks subsequent Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM binding, preventing those subunits from being activated [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">2</xref>]. Thus, phosphorylation allows for a bi-directional control of CaMKII activity.</p><p>In addition to activating CaMKII, Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM binding and phosphorylation at Thr286 expose binding sites on the enzyme for interactions with other proteins. One example of such activity-dependent interactions at synapses is with the N-Methyl-D-Aspartate 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14, particularly the NR2B subunit. The binding of NR2B to activated CaMKII also leads to a similar form of biochemical memory because it prevents the autoinhibitory domain from flipping back on the catalytic region, thereby leading to autonomous activity of CaMKII [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR44">4</xref>]. The interesting distinction for this form of CaMKII autonomy, in comparison to the classical autophosphorylation-dependent autonomy, is that it cannot be reversed by phosphatase activity. Furthermore, this binding interaction between CaMKII and NR2B can switch to a persistent mode after a strong Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM activation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR44">4</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR45">5</xref>], providing a long-lasting form of molecular memory that is ideally suited to sustain ongoing changes in synaptic biochemistry.</p></sec><sec id="Sec102"><title>CaMKII as a Decoder of Calcium Oscillations</title><p>The rules governing Thr286 phosphorylation of individual subunits within CaMKII dodecamers make the enzyme capable of decoding the number and frequency of Ca<sup>2+</sup> spikes. The Thr286 phosphorylation reaction can occur only between two neighboring subunits that have been coincidently activated by Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM binding (Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>). If exposed to brief Ca<sup>2+</sup> spikes, as seen at 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5, the dual binding of Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM to neighboring subunits has a low probability. Upon repetitive spikes, the probability of coincident binding of Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM increases, but only if the spike intervals are sufficiently brief to favor accumulation of bound Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM on the holoenzyme. Thus, above a steep threshold frequency of Ca<sup>2+</sup> oscillations, the number of phosphorylated subunits per holoenzyme increases over time. The differential accumulation of phosphorylated – or autonomous – subunits in a CaMKII dodecamer encodes the number and frequency of Ca<sup>2+</sup> oscillations. The initial fraction of autophosphorylated subunits in CaMKII, the amplitude and duration of individual Ca<sup>2+</sup> spikes and the affinity of different CaMKII subtypes for CaM have all been shown to modulate the frequency response of the enzyme [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR46">6</xref>]. These remarkable features should allow the enzyme to decode the temporal patterns of neuronal activity.</p></sec><sec id="Sec103"><title>Spatiotemporal Regulation of CaMKII</title><p>Specificity in signaling is also achieved by controlling the subcellular location of molecules. The subcellular localization of CaMKII is highly regulated by Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Thus, in response to synaptic or electrical activities, the enzyme translocates rapidly to various neuronal compartments, where it can act on diverse functions. (Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">2</xref>).<fig id="Fig9" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium/Calmodulin-dependent Protein Kinase ll in Neurons. Figure 2</label><caption><p>Multiple sites of CaMKII targeting and activity-dependent translocation in neurons.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e5027" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig9_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig9_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 112779?><?image-md5 0dc36346abff62d02f42e796174bda80?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 562?><?image-original-width 480?><?image-scaled-height 562?><?image-scaled-width 480?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/0dc36346abff/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig9_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig9_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 11866?><?thumb-md5 043ad45532558a3cc936afa588392872?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 117?><?thumb-scaled-width 100?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/043ad4553255/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig9_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>Different subunits, such as α and β, bind to common as well as different targets. These subunits can co-assemble in various ratios within dodecamers, allowing the enzyme to be recruited to an increased number of sites in the cell [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">7</xref>]. Among the multiple sites that CaMKII can probably translocate to, only a few have been characterized, as described below.</p><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Nucleus:</italic> Because of its large multimeric structure, CaMKII cannot enter the nucleus by passive diffusion. However, the kinase has been detected by immunocytochemistry in the nucleus of a variety of cell types. The enzyme thus needs a nuclear localization signal (NLS) or a binding partner that contains one to enter the nucleus. In the brain, only the splice variant α<sub>B</sub>-CaMKII contains a functional NLS. But αKAP, a CaMKII anchoring protein that is derived from the α gene, also contains an NLS. αKAP lacks the catalytic and regulatory domains but contains the association domain. It can thus form holoenzymes with other CaMKII isoforms and can target them to the nucleus. Indeed, only 1 or 2 subunits per holoenzyme are necessary for nuclear translocation of the dodecamer. Functionality of the NLS is also regulated by phosphorylation. For example, autophosphorylation at Thr286 affects its nuclear translocation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">7</xref>].</p><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Membranes:</italic> αKAP contains an N-terminal hydrophobic sequence instead of the standard N-terminal kinase domain. This can support the recruitment of the enzyme to intracellular membranes, like to the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">7</xref>].</p><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Cytoskeleton:</italic> In their non-activated state, β-CaMKII binds to 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 whereas α-CaMKII is predominantly cytosolic. Following activation, β-CaMKII unbinds actin and both subunits can bind to other cytoskeletal components, like 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13. Microtubule-associated proteins, such as Tau, MAP2 and MAP6 are major substrates for CaMKII [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">2</xref>].</p><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Synapses:</italic> CaMKII can translocate to postsynaptic sites during neuronal activity, where the kinase can also bind to several synaptic proteins. Its multivalent structure should in fact allow CaMKII to simultaneously bind several partners (Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">2</xref>). This is particularly relevant in the PSD, where proteins are tightly packed (hence the electron-dense nature) and where CaMKII is particularly abundant. One major activity-dependent binding target of CaMKII at synapses is the NMDA receptor, as described above. This interaction is of particular interest because it can be made persistent above a certain activation threshold, and may lock the enzyme at stimulated synapses [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR45">5</xref>].</p><p>In addition, the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13 of α-, but not β-CaMKII, is transported in dendrites in an activity-dependent manner, where local translation can occur. This enables a rapid and localized delivery of CaMKII proteins to synapses [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR48">8</xref>]. At presynaptic sites, CaMKII is associated with synaptic vesicles and can bind and phosphorylate 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 I [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">2</xref>].</p><p>
<italic toggle="yes">Intracellular clustering:</italic> During ischemia, or during strong stimulation at synapses, CaMKII holoenzymes bind to each other. This process called self-association forms supramolecular aggregates of holoenzymes. Those inter-holoenzyme interactions, which are formed via catalytic and autoinhibitory domains, need activation of the kinase by Ca<sup>2+</sup>/CaM and are regulated by intracellular pH, ATP concentration and autophosphorylation. Aggregates of CaMKII have been observed in vitro as well as in intact cells, both at synaptic and extrasynaptic sites [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR49">9</xref>]. This process could favor additional recruitment of CaMKII at strongly stimulated synapses and might support the formation of post-synaptic scaffolds embedded with multiple CaMKII and binding partners.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec104"><title>CaMKII and Neuronal Function</title><p>CaMKII is implicated in various cellular functions, including the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism, membrane current, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 synthesis and release, cytoskeletal organization, intracellular Ca<sup>2+</sup> homeostasis, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_20, synaptic plasticity and some forms of memory [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>]. Here, we will focus on CaMKII implications in gene regulation and synaptic plasticity.</p><sec id="Sec105"><title>CaMKII and Gene Regulation</title><p>During neuronal activity, Ca<sup>2+</sup> levels increase in the cytosol, but also in the nucleus. The ability of some isoforms of CaMKII to target the nucleus suggests that the enzyme is involved in regulating gene expression. CaMKII can phosphorylate 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_20, like CREB, ATF-1 and NeuroD, and is known to regulate the transcription of the immediate-early gene <italic toggle="yes">c-fos</italic>. To date however, most evidence showing that CaMKII regulates gene expression comes from studies in non-neuronal systems. For example, the first experimental evidence that nuclear localization of CaMKII was required for transcriptional regulation was shown for the gene coding for atrial natriuretic factor in heart tissue [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">1</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">7</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR48">8</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec106"><title>CaMKII and Synaptic Plasticity; Learning and Memory</title><p>CaMKII has attracted the attention of neuroscientists in particular because of its role in synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Studies have been done mostly in the hippocampus, but results from other regions also support the role of CaMKII in synaptic plasticity. Long-term potentiation (LTP) of synaptic transmission is a type of synaptic plasticity that is thought to underlie some forms of learning and memory. Several results indicate that CaMKII, activated by the rise in Ca<sup>2+</sup> that accompanies the high-frequency stimulation required to induce LTP, initiates a biochemical cascade that potentiates synaptic transmission. Indeed, after the induction of LTP, autonomous activity of CaMKII increases. Peptide inhibitors blocking both Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent and -independent activity of CaMKII prevented LTP induction by different protocols. But because of the possible lack of specificity of these inhibitors, the essential role of CaMKII in LTP was only confirmed after the observation of an impaired synaptic potentiation in αCaMKII knockout mice and in mice that express a mutant CaMKII that cannot autophosphorylate at Thr286. Those mice also show deficits in both learning and memory. For instance, preventing CaMKII autophosphorylation was shown to interfere with experience-dependent plasticity, such as spatial learning. Local translation of αCaMKII in dendrites is also important for synaptic plasticity because disrupting the transport of its mRNA impairs LTP and some types of memory. Conversely, instead of inhibiting or removing CaMKII, introducing activated CaMKII in neurons of hippocampal slices can induce LTP [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR48">8</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR50">10</xref>].</p><p>How does CaMKII regulate synaptic transmission? Many mechanisms have been examined, but one good example is its effects on 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1. CaMKII phosphorylates these synaptic receptors, thereby enhancing their conductance, and also leads to the addition of new AMPA receptors into synapses. Both effects contribute to strengthening the synapse [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR48">8</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR50">10</xref>]. But in addition to its signaling effects, CaMKII seems to play a structural role in synaptic plasticity. A recent study demonstrated that β-CaMKII, but not α, was capable of bundling F-actin, independently of its kinase activity. This bundling stabilizes the architecture of dendritic spines and might support dendritic spine remodeling that accompany synaptic plasticity.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec107"><title>Summary</title><p>CaMKII is a multifunctional kinase highly abundant in the brain and critically involved in the regulation of several functions in neurons. Its unusual structural and regulatory properties support its multiple functions by enabling the enzyme to decode specific patterns of Ca<sup>2+</sup> signals in time and in space, for brief and long-lasting effects. Since the discovery of CaMKII by Howard Schulman and colleagues three decades ago, many studies have unraveled some of its functions and mechanisms of action, but many aspects are still unresolved. Nevertheless, what we have learned so far about this enzyme has contributed to a better understanding of how signaling in cells can be achieved with specificity, multiplicity, efficiency, and persistence.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec108"><title>Calcium Channel Blocker</title><sec id="Sec109"><title>Definition</title><p>A family of clinically used compounds that block the L-type Cav1.2 calcium channel and relaxes smooth muscle.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec110"><title>Calcium Channelopathies</title><sec id="Sec111"><title>Definition</title><p>One type of ion <xref rid="Sec110" ref-type="sec">Channelopathies</xref> leading to neurological disorders in vertebrates including humans. Since rises in intracellular Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentration [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sub>i</sub> regulate or initiate a plethora of intracellular events including metabolic processes, secretion of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 and hormones, muscle contraction, cell differentiation and gene expression, and since these [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sub>i</sub> rises are largely generated by influx into the intracellular medium via voltage-gated L-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels, genetic dysfunctions of these channels cause multifarious neurological diseases, including 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8 (loss of muscle strength), failures in muscle 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1, congenital stationary night blindness, or malignant hyperthermic sensitivity.</p><p>

</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec112"><title>Calcium Channels — An Overview</title><sec id="Sec113"><title>Definition</title><p>Voltage-gated Ca<sup>2±</sup> channels are integral membrane proteins forming aqueous pores which open in response to cell depolarization. Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels play a key role in controlling vital functions: they shape the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 and membrane electrical oscillations and act as gate-controller of Ca<sup>2+</sup>, the most ubiquitous 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR51">1</xref>]. As such, Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels are implicated in cardiac, skeletal and smooth 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13 (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5), 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8 and neurotransmitter release (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5) and Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent processes that modulate short- and long-term cell activity and gene expression (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_5) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR52">2</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55">5</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec114"><title>Characteristics</title><p>Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels have been grouped into two main classes, based on their threshold of activation: the high voltage-activated (HVA) channels and the low voltage-activated (LVA) channels [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR54">4</xref>]; although this classification could not be strictly applied since some of the HVA channels activate at significantly low voltages [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR52">2</xref>]. LVA channels activate “ transiently” during small depolarizations near 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_18 (→ 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13) and are therefore commonly indicated as T-type channels. T-type channels are responsible for 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12, oscillatory cell activity, muscle contraction, hormone release, cell growth, differentiation and proliferation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55">5</xref>]. The HVA channels require larger membrane depolarizations to open and are further subdivided into four types (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_20) based on their structural, pharmacological and biophysical characteristics [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR52">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR53">3</xref>]. They are responsible for the sustained depolarizing phase of action potentials, muscle contraction, hormone and neurotransmitter release, gene expression and cell differentiation.</p><sec id="Sec115"><title>Molecular Structure</title><p>The principal pore-forming subunit of both LVA and HVA channels is the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit, a high- molecular weight protein (190–250 kDa), which is structurally similar to the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 α-subunit [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR51">1</xref>]. It is formed by four domains (<italic toggle="yes">I–IV</italic>) linked together in a single polypeptide chain and each domain contains six putative transmembrane segments (S1<italic toggle="yes">–</italic>S6), plus a loop (P) that dips partially into the pore to form the pore-lining region (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">1</xref>). The cytoplasmic loops linking the four domains are structurally important for their interactions with β-subunits, second messengers, membrane binding proteins and channel 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_7.<fig id="Fig10" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Channels — An Overview. Red cylinders indicate the positively charged S4 segments (voltage sensors), and the thick green lines denote the pore loops (P) that line the permeation pathway for Ca<sup>2+</sup>. </p><p>Molecular cloning of Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels has provided evidence for the existence of ten different pore-forming α<sub>1</sub> subunits with pharmacological and biophysical profiles similar to the endogenous Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels expressed in most tissues. Alignment of their amino acid sequences suggests strong homologies and divergences between the various Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel types (Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">2</xref>). Strong homologies exist between the four L-types (Cav1), the N-, P/Q- and R-type (Ca<sub>v</sub>2), and the three T-type (Ca<sub>v</sub>3) channels, while large divergences exist between the HVA and LVA subfamilies. The LVA family includes three genes encoding the Ca<sub>v</sub>3.1–Ca<sub>v</sub>3.3 channels. </p><p>At variance with the T-type channels, whose α<sub>1</sub>-subunit is sufficient to warrant 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 and 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_9, channel expression and membrane incorporation, the HVA channels are hetero-multimeric protein complexes which comprise the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit in association with auxiliary β, α<sub>2</sub>-δ and γ-subunits (Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">3</xref>). Coexpression of α<sub>2</sub>-δ with the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit ensures proper Ca<sup>2+</sup> current kinetics and current densities. The same occurs with the co-expression of β and α<sub>1</sub>-subunits. Still vague is the role of γ-subunits (γ<sub>1</sub> to γ<sub>8</sub>) which consist of four transmembrane domains and whose site of interaction with the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit is still unknown. The α<sub>2</sub>-δ-subunit is formed by a membrane-spanning δ-peptide (27 kDa) and an extracellular α<sub>2</sub>-peptide (143 kDa) bound together by a disulfide bridge (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">1</xref>). Presently, four genes encoding for different α<sub>2</sub>-δ-subunits (α<sub>2</sub>-δ<sub>1</sub> to α<sub>2</sub>-δ<sub>4</sub>) have been identified with several additional splice variants. The up-regulation of the α<sub>2</sub>-δ gene appears to correlate with the onset of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 (non-noxious stimuli eliciting pain) and ligands that target the α<sub>2</sub>-δ-subunit, the gabapentins, are used for treatment of neuropathic pain. The four β-subunits (β<sub>1</sub> to β<sub>4</sub>) and their splice variants so far identified are almost exclusively cytosolic. They possess a hydrophobic region containing SH3 and guanylate kinase domains, indicating that they belong to the membrane-associated guanylate kinase (MAGUK) family and as such may integrate multiple signaling pathways near the channel. The β-subunit has high-affinity for a conserved region within the domain I-II region of N- and PQ-type channels, termed the <italic toggle="yes">alpha interaction domain</italic> (AID).<fig id="Fig12" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Channels — An Overview. </p></sec><sec id="Sec116"><title>Activation-Inactivation Gating</title><p>As for other voltage-gated ion channels, the probability of Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels opening is strictly voltage-dependent, i.e., the switch from a closed (non-conductive) to an open (conductive) configuration is strictly dependent on voltage, usually requiring 4–8 mV to change e-fold the probability of channel opening [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR56">6</xref>]. Structure-function studies have associated this property to the presence of positively charged lysine and arginine residues distributed in the S4 transmembrane segment of each domain, which form the “ 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_22 ” (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">1</xref>). However, the exact location of the activation gates that regulate the open and closed states of the pore remains unknown.</p><p>During maintained depolarization, Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels tend to inactivate, but the speed and extent of channel inactivation may vary dramatically. In general, Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels inactivate by either Ca<sup>2+</sup>- or voltage-dependent mechanisms. Ca<sup>2+</sup> -dependent inactivation is dominant for the cardiac Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2 L-type channel, but may also occur for other HVA channels. Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent inactivation is a <xref rid="Sec137" ref-type="sec">calmodulin</xref>-dependent process, involving sites on the C-terminal domain of the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit. Voltage-dependent inactivation is a general term for inactivation that does not clearly depend on Ca<sup>2+</sup>. T-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels tend to inactivate rapidly and almost completely, while inactivation of HVA channels is usually slow and incomplete. Spontaneous switch between inactivating and non-inactivating modes have been observed in single N-type channels, perhaps reflecting modulation by some intracellular signaling process. However, how Ca<sup>2+</sup>-binding or membrane voltage affect the inactivation gate is still widely unknown [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR56">6</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec117"><title>Channel Permeability</title><p>The present view of Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel permeability is based on the existence of an intrapore binding site controlling both ion selectivity and channel block: the selectivity filter. This highly specialized region of Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels consists of a ring of four negative charged groups inside the pore. In HVA channels, each of the four P loops contains a glutamate forming the EEEE locus, in T-type channels two glutamates are substituted by two aspartates in the corresponding position (EEDD locus). The spatial arrangement of the four negative charges in the P loops is postulated to closely coordinate two Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions whose sequential entrance and subsequent interaction induce high Ca<sup>2+</sup> fluxes while preserving high affinity for the pore-site [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR57">7</xref>]. Although this simple ion-ion interaction would explain the dual nature of Ca<sup>2+</sup> as permeant ions at millimolar concentrations and as blockers of Na<sup>+</sup> currents at micromolar concentrations, the complete understanding of Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel permeability is likely to require a further hypothesis of ion-pore structure interactions. The recent availability of T-type channel clones [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55">5</xref>] has allowed closer comparisons between LVA and HVA channel permeability properties, highlighting the role that the EEEE or EEDD locus play in the regulation of ion selectivity in the two channel groups. Ca<sub>v</sub>3.1 T-type channels have apparently a narrower pore size (5.1 Å diameter) compared to the Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2 L-type pore size (6.2 Å diameter) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR57">7</xref>]. This structural difference may explain the different Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Ba<sup>2+</sup> selectivity and blocking action of Cd<sup>2+</sup> and Ni<sup>2+</sup> of the two channel families (LVA and HVA): the L-, N- and P/Q-type channels being more permeable to Ba<sup>2+</sup> than Ca<sup>2+</sup> and more sensitive to the block by Cd<sup>2+</sup> and the T-type channels being equally permeable to Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Ba<sup>2+</sup> and more sensitive to the block by Ni<sup>2+</sup> (Table <xref rid="Tab2" ref-type="table">1</xref>).<table-wrap id="Tab2" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Channels — An Overview. </p></sec><sec id="Sec118"><title>Physiology, Pharmacology and Channelopathies</title><p>In the following paragraphs are described the tissue and cellular location, physiological role, pharmacology and related <xref rid="Sec110" ref-type="sec">Channelopathies</xref> associated to each Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel type as summarized in Table <xref rid="Tab2" ref-type="table">1</xref>.</p><p>L-type channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>1)<bold><italic toggle="yes">.</italic></bold> L-type channels are widely expressed in many tissues and control a number of Ca<sup>2+</sup>-dependent responses in excitable cells. In central neurons they are preferentially located on proximal dendrites and cell bodies and are involved in postsynaptic integration, neuronal plasticity, gene transcription and mood behavior. In sensory neurons (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_8), they directly control neurotransmitter release and sensory perception. The L-type family includes four α<sub>1</sub>-subunits (Ca<sub>v</sub>1.1 to Ca<sub>v</sub>1.4) with different structure-function characteristics but common blockers: 1,4-dihydropyridines (DHPs), phenylalkylamines and benzothiazepines. With the exception of Ca<sub>v</sub>1.3 and Ca<sub>v</sub>1.4, which activate at relatively low voltages, the other Ca<sub>v</sub>1 channels activate at voltages much more positive than resting potential. Activation is fast and sharply voltage-dependent while inactivation is relatively slow in the presence of Ba<sup>2+</sup> but speeds-up in the presence of Ca<sup>2+</sup> (Ca<sup>2±</sup>-dependent inactivation). Deactivation (giving rise to 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_20) is also fast, ensuring rapid closing of the channels on membrane repolarization to resting levels. L-type channels are distinguished from the other Ca<sub>v</sub> channels by their high sensitivity to DHPs. DHP antagonists (nifedipine, nitrendipine) reversibly block the channels and help quantifying the amount of L-type channels expressed in a cell, while DHP agonists (Bay K 8644) prolong the open state of the channel, producing slow tail currents near resting potential. As such, DHP agonists allow measuring the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 of high conductance L-type channels in membrane patches, otherwise hardly detectable [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR58">8</xref>]. L-type channels can be often distinguished from the other Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels for their <xref rid="Sec150" ref-type="sec">cAMP/PKA-mediated up-regulation</xref> which causes increased mean open times and probability of openings at the single channel level and increased Ca<sup>2+</sup> current amplitude in whole-cell recordings [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR59">9</xref>]. Neuronal and neuroendocrine L-type channels can be also inhibited by a fast 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_7 mechanism activated by neurotransmitters which could be at the basis of an 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1 of hormone release.</p><p>P/Q-type channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1)<bold>.</bold> The Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1 family includes two Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels which are nearly indistinguishable except for their different affinity to a common blocker: the spider venom ω-agatoxin IVA. P-type channels are more sensitive to ω-agatoxin IVA (K<sub>d</sub> 1–3 nM) than Q-type channels (K<sub>d</sub> 100–200 nM). Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1 channels are widely expressed in neurons but are also available in pancreatic, pituitary and chromaffin cells. Their main physiological function is to control neurotransmitter release in central neurons and mammalian 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 where they are highly expressed at the presynaptic sites. P/Q-type channels control also the excitation-secretion coupling in pancreatic and chromaffin cells. Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1 channels play a key role in neurotransmitter release due to their high-density of expression at the release sites of central synapses and share most of the modulatory properties of N-type channels described below. Similarly to the N-type channels they bind tightly to the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 proteins at the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19 of the II-III linker of the channel. P/Q-type channels are also effectively inhibited by the neurotransmitter activated GPCRs mechanism described below. Missense mutations of P/Q-type channels cause 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_6 associated to an apparent gain of function as a result of an increased probability of channel openings and alteration of synaptic transmission (Table <xref rid="Tab2" ref-type="table">1</xref>).</p><p>N-type channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>2.2). Ca<sub>v</sub>2.2 channels are widely expressed in the central and peripheral nervous system and chromaffin cells. They are highly expressed at the nerve terminals, where they control neurotransmitter release, and to a minor degree at the dendritic sites, where they are involved in Ca<sup>2+</sup> signaling. Ca<sub>v</sub>2.2 channels control also hormone release in neuroendocrine cells. The channels activate at relatively high voltages. Maximal activation at positive potentials and deactivation on return to resting levels are both fast. Inactivation is variable but significantly faster than L-type channels and slower than T-type channels. Ca<sub>v</sub>2.2 channels are insensitive to DHPs but are selectively blocked by ω-conotoxin GVIA and related cone snail toxins (Table <xref rid="Tab2" ref-type="table">1</xref>).</p><p>N-type channels play a key role in neurotransmitter release due to their high-density of expression at the release sites and their tight binding to the SNARE complex of the vesicle release machinery (syntaxin 1A, SNAP-25, VAMP2/synaptobrevin and synaptotagmin). These proteins bind at the synprint motif of the II-III linker of the channel and the tight interaction affects the availability and gating of the channel. The SNARE complex in fact either steadily inactivates the channel or inhibits its activation through a G<sub>βγ</sub> subunit. Interestingly, N-type channels are effectively modulated by GPCRs activated by neurotransmitters and the mechanism is thought to be at the basis of 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_16. Briefly, an activated G<sub>βγ</sub> subunit binds directly to the pore-forming α<sub>1</sub>-subunit of the N-type channel and shifts the gating mode from “willing” (from which the channel readily opens) to “reluctant” (from which the channel opens less frequently). The modulatory mechanism is 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13, voltage-dependent and causes an increased delay of the channel opening which produces an overall slow activation of the “reluctant” channel. Strong depolarizations opening the channels reduce the affinity of G<sub>βγ</sub> for the α<sub>1</sub>-subunit and the channel recovers its normal gating mode.</p><p>R-type channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3). Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3 channels are widely expressed in the central nervous system at the cell bodies, dendrites and presynaptic terminals. They are also expressed in 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13, heart, pituitary and chromaffin cells. The Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3 channel has been originally reported to encode a Ca<sup>2+</sup> channel type with biophysical properties between LVA and HVA channels, or usually as an HVA channel resistant to DHPs, ω-toxins and thus called R-type (for “residual”). Ca<sub>v</sub>3 channels are likely to form a family of several channels with fast activation but variable inactivation that could be fast and comparable to the Ca<sub>v</sub>3 types or slow like the Ca<sub>v</sub>1 channels. They are involved in neurotransmitter and hormone release, repetitive firing (→ 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_1) and 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12. The tarantula toxin SNX-482 blocks exogenously expressed Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3 currents but is only partially or not effective on native R-type currents, suggesting that Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3 does not always conduct a significant portion of the R-type current which remains after blocking all the other voltage-gated Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels. Ca<sub>v</sub>2.3 channels are also sensitive to small doses of Ni<sup>2+</sup>. In some case the Ni<sup>2+</sup> block has K<sub>d</sub> comparable to that of the Ca<sub>v</sub>3.2 T-type channel described below.</p><p>T-type channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>3). Ca<sub>v</sub>3 channels (Ca<sub>v</sub>3.1 to Ca<sub>v</sub>3.3) are ubiquitously expressed and sustain key physiological functions which derive from their unique properties [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR54">4</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55">5</xref>]: (i) they activate and inactivate at unusually negative voltages and are responsible for a window-current near resting potentials, (ii) they exhibit fast and complete inactivation during sustained depolarization and deactivate slowly on repolarization, (iii) they are equally or slightly more permeable to Ca<sup>2+</sup> than Ba<sup>2+</sup> and have small single channel conductance, (iv) they outlast 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13 and (v) they are preferentially blocked by low doses of mibefradil and Ni<sup>2+</sup> (particularly the Ca<sub>v</sub>3.2) (Table <xref rid="Tab2" ref-type="table">1</xref>). At present, Ca<sub>v</sub>3 channels are recognized to play a critical role in many physiological functions in which a low-threshold Ca<sup>2+</sup> entry is required to trigger, or sustain, specific cell activities. This is particularly true for the generation of low-threshold spikes, pacemaking activity, hormone secretion, cell growth and differentiation. T-type channels play also a critical role in several pathologies in which either their recruitment, overexpression, or altered gating cause cardiac hypertrophy, hypertension, heart failure, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12, 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14, and 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_16. Most recently, T-type channels are shown to control the vesicular release of neurotransmitters in neurons, and very recent data indicate that they are involved in fast <xref rid="Sec235" ref-type="sec">catecholamine</xref> release in adrenal chromaffin cells.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec119"><title>Calcium Channels: Regulation of Gene Transcription</title><sec id="Sec120"><title>Synonyms</title><p>Excitation-transcription coupling; Voltage-gated calcium channels/ligand-gated calcium channels and control of gene expression; Calcium-regulated nuclear signaling</p></sec><sec id="Sec121"><title>Definition</title><p>Nerve activity induces Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx through voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), and activates vital functions such as 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 (NT) and gene transcription. The latter function is often coupled to permanent changes to the structure of synapses (e.g., 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_19) and the survivability of neurons. Recent research indicate that the specificity of local nuclear signaling pathways depends upon the association of specific channel types to cytosolic Ca<sup>2+</sup>-sensitive factors and not just Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx <italic toggle="yes">per se</italic>. Indeed, it is only the L-type (Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2) channels which are critical for the transcriptional regulation of many genes and these contribute only to a fraction of the total Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx during neural activity. Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx by other means, such as the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14, also contribute to calcium-dependent gene expression changes and share many but not all of the same nuclear signaling pathways.</p></sec><sec id="Sec122"><title>Characteristics</title><sec id="Sec123"><title>Calcium as a Signaling Molecule</title><p>The nervous system relies on charged molecules to relay information. Whereas the relatively inert Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> ions serve mostly to establish membrane potential and carry action potentials along excitable membranes, Ca<sup>2+</sup> has properties that allow it to accomplish additional functions. First, it has a unique affinity for binding ligands containing oxygen-donating groups such as carboxyls, carbonyls, ethers, and alcohols. Second, Ca<sup>2+</sup> is kept at low levels within the cytosol since it precipitates organic anions and is toxic to cells at high concentrations. These features likely lead to the exploitation of the calcium ion not only as a charge carrier but also as a signaling molecule.</p></sec><sec id="Sec124"><title>Calcium-regulated Genes</title><p>Nerve activity promotes subcellular calcium “hotspots” or microdomains around individual channels, and collectively these active channels contribute to global cellular processes including synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival. An example is long-term memory which involves synaptic connectivity changes activated via 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12. Strengthening of synapses induced by LTP requires gene transcription mediated by calcium-sensitive signaling pathways [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61">1</xref>]. Furthermore, activity-dependent neuronal survival, which is important during cognitive development, also requires calcium-dependent gene transcription [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62">2</xref>].</p><p>“First responder” genes are termed 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_9, whose transcription is upregulated without a requirement for newly synthesized proteins. The expression of IEGs is tightly regulated in space and time in active neurons by the summation of nerve inputs and local Ca<sup>2+</sup> flux. 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_2 is a classical calcium-activated IEG that mediates activity-dependent neuronal survival and is required for establishment of LTP (reviewed in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63">3</xref>]). BDNF is a neurotrophin that activates downstream signaling pathways through binding to 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_18 and low affinity receptor p75 (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_16) to exert immediate and long term effects on synaptic activity. Not surprisingly, mutations in the BDNF gene have been correlated with neuronal dysfunction including impaired episodic memory [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63">3</xref>]. Numerous other genes encoding transcription factors, growth factors, cytoskeletal proteins, and proteins involved in signaling and metabolism have also been classified as IEGs including <italic toggle="yes">c-fos, fos B, c-jun, jun B, zif268, Egr-3, Cox-2, Rheb, Arc, Narp, β-activin, Homer</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">nur77</italic>; many have been implicated in aspects of neuronal development and survival, and synaptic plasticity changes [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62">2</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR64">4</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec125"><title>Calcium-mediated Cell Signaling</title><p>Calcium signaling depends on a cascade of electrochemical and biochemical events. These include stimulus sensation and opening of a channel or receptor and influx of Ca<sup>2+</sup> into the cytosol, binding of Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions to intracellular ligands, and signaling to terminal effectors. Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx occurs along steep electrochemical gradients across the plasma membrane, through highly-selective channels or receptors including VGCCs and NMDA receptors, or from intracellular stores through ryanodine and inositol 1, 4, 5-triphosphate receptors (IP<sub>3</sub>). Cytosolic Ca<sup>2+</sup> is quickly buffered and limited to transient microdomains (<xref rid="Sec23" ref-type="sec">Calcium Microdomains</xref>) surrounding the pores of open channels (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>).<fig id="Fig13" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Calcium Channels: Regulation of Gene Transcription. Figure 1</label><caption><p>(a) Illustration of the subunit complex of high voltage-activated calcium channels. Calmodulin or CaM (shown in red) containing EF-hand motifs, bind the C-terminus of the α<sub>1</sub> subunits of calcium channels. (b) Cleaved C-termini of Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2 channels translocate to the nucleus to activate gene transcription. A β<sub>4</sub> subunit isoform also translocates to the nucleus and interacts with nuclear factors involved in gene expression. (c) L-type channels mediate Ca<sup>2+</sup> signaling via CaM bound to their C-termini. CaM is activated by Ca<sup>2+</sup> entry through L-type (Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2) channels and mediates both calcium-dependent inactivation and gene transcription.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="d32e6665" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig13_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig13_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 49723?><?image-md5 bc56ac4f6ab214014f36faa6a0027ecb?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-original-height 239?><?image-original-width 480?><?image-scaled-height 239?><?image-scaled-width 480?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/bc56ac4f6ab2/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig13_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig13_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 12523?><?thumb-md5 fd7cddd7046dfcc39836479e4590d0ec?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 160?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/5838/7163932/fd7cddd7046d/978-3-540-29678-2_3_Fig13_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig>
</p><p>Consequently, calcium-sensing signaling molecules must be in close proximity or directly coupled to channels. Voltage-gated L-type channels, which are important for coupling excitation with transcriptional changes in the nucleus, are localized in the proximal dendrites and cell soma where they are positioned to both sense incoming waves of depolarization originating in the dendrites and to signal to the nucleus.</p></sec><sec id="Sec126"><title>Calcium-sensitive, Nuclear Signaling Pathways</title><p>Calcium/cAMP Response Element Binding protein (<xref rid="Sec1717" ref-type="sec">CREB</xref>) is a transcription factor whose activity is implicated in calcium-related signaling events and is activated through phosphorylation of a serine residue (Ser-133). Cytosolic Ca<sup>2+</sup> microdomains trigger CREB phosphorylation via several pathways with distinct temporal kinetics, the most significant of which are the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_13 and the <xref rid="Sec96" ref-type="sec">calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase</xref>Pathway (<xref rid="Sec145" ref-type="sec">CaMK</xref>) (reviewed in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63">3</xref>], Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>). Whereas the CaMK pathway is involved in early phosphorylation of CREB, the Ras/MAPK pathway is required for sustained CREB phosphorylation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65">5</xref>]. Both pathways are critical since a sustained CREB phosphorylation is required for transcriptional activation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65">5</xref>]. Phosphorylated CREB promotes transcription of a variety of IEGs including BDNF and mediates both activity-dependent neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63">3</xref>].</p><p>Besides CREB, additional calcium-dependent transcription factors have been identified. Like CREB, these are typically regulated by CaM or downstream members of the CaM signaling pathway, and translocate to the nucleus upon activation. These include:<list list-type="order"><list-item><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14: NF-AT has been implicated in synaptic plasticity [reviewed in <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66">6</xref>]. NF-AT translocates to the nucleus upon dephosphorylation by calcineurin, a protein phosphatase controlled by the CaMK pathway.</p></list-item><list-item><p>Myocyte Enhancer Factor 2: MEF2 is involved in neuronal survival and apoptosis. Phosphorylation of MEF2 via the Ras/MAPK pathway leads to transcription of MEF2-regulated genes that promote survival of cerebellar granule neurons. During T-cell receptor mediated apoptosis, MEF2 activation via the calcium/CaM pathway leads to the expression of the pro-apoptotic IEG Nur77 [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62">2</xref>]. MEF2 can also be cleaved by calcium-activated caspase enzymes, generating pro-apoptotic, dominant-interfering forms that bind DNA to inhibit MEF2 transcription.</p></list-item><list-item><p>
10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14: NF-κB promotes neuronal survival by transcribing genes that inhibit apoptosis such as manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), Inhibitors of APoptosis (IAPs), and the Bcl-2 homologue Bfl-1/A1 [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR67">7</xref>]. Calcium/CaM mediated dissociation of an inhibitory subunit from the NF-κB hetero-trimeric complex leads to nuclear localization of a transcriptionally active hetero-dimer [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR67">7</xref>]. NF-κB has also been implicated in synaptic plasticity changes and spatial learning [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR67">7</xref>].</p></list-item><list-item><p>Downstream Regulatory Element-Antagonist Modulator: 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_4 contains four EF-hand motifs for binding Ca<sup>2+</sup>, and acts as a nuclear transcriptional repressor that binds to regulatory DRE motifs of target genes in conditions of low calcium. Genes regulated by DREAM include the IEG <italic toggle="yes">c-fos</italic> and Prodynorphin, a transcription factor involved in memory acquisition and pain [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68">8</xref>]. Interestingly, in the absence of nuclear Ca<sup>2+</sup>, DREAM binds CREB and prevents it from recruiting <xref rid="Sec1717" ref-type="sec">CREB Binding Protein</xref> (CBP), a factor critical for CREB-mediated transcriptional activation.</p></list-item></list>
</p></sec><sec id="Sec127"><title>L-type calcium channels and control of gene expression</title><p>Of the known VGCCs in the nervous system (i.e., Ca<sub>v</sub>1 (L-type), Ca<sub>v</sub>2 (N-, P/Q-, R-types), and Ca<sub>v</sub>3 (T-type)), L-types are the only channel type established to couple excitation with transcription. Selectively blocking L-type channels with dihydropyridines inhibits the expression of many IEGs. Intracellular microdomains of Ca<sup>2+</sup> generated by L-type channels lead to both nuclear signaling and negative feedback regulation of channel gating itself by means of calcium-dependent inactivation. It has been reported that both processes are dependent on the tethering of calcium-sensitive molecules to the channel where they can sense the local increase in calcium concentration. CaM, a cytosolic protein able to directly bind calcium via its EF-hand motifs, remains tethered to L-type (Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2) channels via an isoleucine-glutamine (IQ) motif in the channel’s C-terminus. Disrupting either the ability of CaM to interact with L-type channels or CaM’s ability to bind Ca<sup>2+</sup> leads to loss of calcium-dependent inactivation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69">9</xref>] (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>). Subsequent research from Dolmetsch and colleagues illustrates that CaM also mediates nuclear signaling by L-type channels [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65">5</xref>] (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>). This research group assayed the phosphorylation of CREB and activation of the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway in neurons where endogenous L-type channels had been blocked by dihydropyridines. By transfecting functional drug-resistant L-type channels into cultured primary neurons, Dolmetsch et al. showed that mutating the CaM-binding IQ motif or co-expressing calcium-insensitive CaM abrogated calcium-dependent activation of the Ras/MAPK pathway, CREB phosphorylation, and activation of MEF2. As illustrated in Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1c</xref>, this research establishes CaM as a pivotal regulatory center for L-type channels, in channel self-regulation and the feed-forward control of gene expression.</p><p>Some intriguing twists in the story of how L-type channels modulate gene transcription are now emerging. The C-terminus of Ca<sub>v</sub>1.2 translocates to the nucleus as a ~75 kDa peptide (termed CCAT) after proteolytic cleavage at the cell membrane. In the nucleus, CCAT peptide binds transcriptional regulator p54(nrb)/NonO, associates with endogenous promoters, and promotes a significant up-regulation of 16 genes (e.g., axon guidance factor 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14 and gap junction protein Cx31.1) and down-regulation of 31 genes (e.g., 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14and the 10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_14Scl8A1) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70">10</xref>] (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1b</xref>). Nuclear translocation of CCAT is observed in several central neuron types, especially in adults and heterologous expression of CCAT promotes increased neurite outgrowth in cultured primary neurons. Interestingly, CCAT translocation requires low cytosolic Ca<sup>2+</sup> levels suggesting a mode of transcriptional regulation unlike the CaM dependent pathway which requires Ca<sup>2+</sup> and neuronal activity. It has been suggested that a CCAT-like cleavage mechanism may be widely applicable since the C-terminus of the P/Q-type channel (Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1) is also cleaved and translocates to the nucleus; yet, it remains to be determined whether truncated Ca<sub>v</sub>2.1 peptides affect gene expression.</p><p>With the exception of T-type channels, the pore-forming α<sub>1</sub> subunits of VGCCs associate with accessory subunits (termed α<sub>2</sub>, δ, β, and γ) which significantly modulate the electrophysiological properties and surface expression of the α<sub>1</sub> subunits (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1a</xref>). Recent evidence suggests that a short β<sub>4</sub> isoform translocates to the nucleus and interacts with heterochromatin protein 1γ to promote gene silencing, however the underlying mechanisms and significance remains to be elucidated (Fig. <xref rid="Fig13" ref-type="fig">1b</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="Sec128"><title>Control of Gene Expression by NMDA, Ryanodine, and IP<sub>3</sub> Receptors</title><p>Calcium flux through post-synaptic NMDA receptors shares many of the downstream targets as L-type calcium channels to promote gene expression and neuronal survival. The similarities with L-type channels include activating CREB by phosphorylation, promoting the expression of some IEGs [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68">8</xref>], and nuclear signaling via the CaMK and the Ras/MAPK signaling pathways. It has been reported that different calcium sources may be required for different phases of gene transcriptional activation. In particular, the NMDA receptors mediate an earlier phase of CREB phosphorylation (i.e., 10 min after depolarization), while the L-type channels are required in later stages. NMDA receptors also operate through downstream effectors associated with LTP induction, that do not overlap with L-type calcium channels. For example, EphB receptor tyrosine kinases localize at excitatory synapses and enhance the expression of NMDA receptor-mediated genes, but not those mediated by L-type channels. Interestingly, variations in the composition or location of the NMDA receptors create highly divergent signaling. Whereas synaptic NMDA receptors mediate neuronal survival, calcium entry via extra-synaptic receptors inhibits CREB phosphorylation and promotes cell death. Furthermore, changes in the composition of NMDA receptor subunit alters MAPK pathway signaling leading to either LTP or LTD (10.1007/978-3-540-29678-2_12).</p><p>Internal calcium sources may also participate in regulating gene transcription, but there is not much evidence for this mechanism occurring in neurons. IP<sub>3</sub> receptor activity can mediate the phosphorylation of CREB and activate NF-AT and NF-κB transcription factors in both muscle and neuronal cells (reviewed in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66">6</xref>]). Ryanodine receptor-mediated Ca<sup>2+</sup> influx has been linked to activation of the transcription factor NF-AT and expression of the slow myosin heavy chain I gene in muscle (reviewed in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66">6</xref>]).</p></sec><sec id="Sec129"><title>Conclusion</title><p>Gene transcriptional changes are the capacity of neurons to adapt to changing conditions, such as to modify their structure, their survivability and enhancement of connectivity. Regulation of gene expression is necessary in neural development, for the process of learning and memory, and for apoptosis. Importantly, regulatory mechanisms may be harnessed for possible treatment of neurodegenerative disease.</p><p>Specificity in gene regulation is governed by nerve activity and calcium flux. Different calcium sources mediated through L-type calcium channels as well as NMDA receptors and intracellular sources converge through multiple, and often overlapping, signaling pathways (e.g., CREB, CaMK, Ras/MAPK and cAMP dependent protein kinase A (reviewed in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63">3</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66">6</xref>])). These likely contribute collectively to global cellular changes in nuclear Ca<sup>2+</sup> to enhance the transcription of IEGs. At a local level, calcium is sensed by tethered CaM at the C-terminus of L-type calcium channels. CaM serves as a regulatory control point for tuning up or down calcium channel activity and its downstream regulators of gene transcription. Interestingly, low calcium also appears to be a signal for gene expression, as both the transcriptional modulator DREAM as well as the C-terminal cleavage product CCAT of L-type channels, require low nuclear and cytosolic Ca<sup>2+</sup> levels respectively for activation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68">8</xref>,<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70">10</xref>]. Future experimentation will further clarify how the varied signaling mechanisms activated by calcium, coming through calcium channels or other sources (eg. NMDA receptors), contribute to the regulation of gene transcription.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="Sec130"><title>Calcium Chelator</title><sec id="Sec131"><title>Definition</title><p>Calcium ions have a double positive charge. Calcium chelators are molecules that bind calcium and cover the ion in a way that it is no longer available for cellular metabolism. It was the invention of calcium chelators that allowed understanding the role of calcium in biological cells, because calcium concentrations in cells are so low that it is impossible to create artificial solutions with lower calcium concentrations unless calcium is removed using chelators. The event of calcium chelators, that can be titrated to create known calcium concentrations, made this ion accessible to direct experimental analysis.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec132"><title>Calcium-regulated Nuclear Signaling</title><p>
